title: Tapering for marathon and cardiac autonomic function
authors: Hug B, Heyer L, Naef N, Buchheit M, Wehrlin JP, Millet GP
population: 9 male runners (marathon training) in a 3-week overload then 3-week taper
findings: 9 male runners followed 3 weeks of overload then 3 weeks of tapering (-33 +/- 7% volume); exhaustive running test (Tlim) and post-exercise heart rate recovery (HRR) and vagal HRV indices (RMSSD) were measured.
Tlim did not change during overload (603 +/- 105 vs 614 +/- 132 s; P = 0.992) but increased (727 +/- 185 s; P = 0.035) during the second week of tapering.
RMSSD(5-10 min) was reduced after the 2nd week of tapering compared with overload (7.6 +/- 3.3 vs 8.6 +/- 2.9 ms; P = 0.045).

Improvements in Tlim during taper correlated negatively with change in HRR(60 s) (r = -0.84; P = 0.005) but not RMSSD (r = -0.21; P = 0.59); authors conclude slower HRR may indicate improved performance and single-day post-exercise HRV monitoring may have little or no additive value.
limitations: Nine runners, single-group design, post-exercise (not resting) autonomic measures on a single day; measurement protocol unlikely to match wearable overnight HRV.
implications: Do not assume that a fall in post-exercise HRV during the taper signals a problem or predicts performance; HRV-based taper flags should require corroboration (symptoms, resting HR, sleep) before an alert.
Performance gain appeared in the second taper week, consistent with a 2-week minimum.
